Why Owl Hoots at Night
Long ago, Owl was awake all day. He loved to talk, and his voice was very loud. Whenever Magpie began to sing, Owl hooted over the top of her song.
The other birds grew cross. They flew up high to the Sun and asked for help.
The Sun called Owl to the tallest tree. "The day belongs to the singers," said the Sun. "If you wish to hoot, you must wait until I sleep."
Owl grumbled, but he agreed. And that is why, even today, owls sleep in the daytime and hoot under the moon.
QuestionText: Who did the birds ask for help?
AnswerA: the Moon
AnswerD: Owl

Ollie looked through his new telescope. A tiny red dot glowed in the night sky.
'That's Mars,' said Dad. 'It looks red because its soil is full of rust.'

Gift of the River
Long ago, the ancient Egyptians lived beside a mighty river called the Nile. All around them was dry, sandy desert.
Each year, the Nile flooded. When the water went down, it left behind thick, black mud. This mud was perfect for growing wheat, onions and other food.
Farmers dug ditches to carry river water to their fields. People also caught fish and used tall reeds called papyrus to make boats and paper.
Without the Nile, Egypt would have been a land of sand and dust. The river was the beating heart of Egypt.
QuestionText: What did the Nile leave behind after it flooded?
AnswerA: thick, black mud
AnswerD: tall, green reeds

Sliding Down the Red Dune
Kira woke while the stars were still out. 'Hurry,' said Uncle Ray. 'We must go before the sun gets high.'
They drove to the biggest dune near town. Kira carried a flat plastic board up the soft red sand. Her feet sank with every step. At the top, she sat on the board and pushed off. Whoosh! She flew to the bottom.
They slid again and again. By nine o'clock, the sand was burning Kira's toes. Uncle Ray packed up the boards. 'Time for a cold drink in the shade,' he said.
QuestionText: What did Kira carry up the dune?
AnswerA: a cold drink
AnswerD: a big umbrella

ComprehensionText:
How a Scrape Heals
Seeing blood on your knee can be scary. But your body knows just what to do.
First, the blood at the top of the scrape gets thick and sticky. This is called a clot. It stops more blood from leaking out.
Next, the clot dries and turns into a hard, brown scab. The scab is like a tiny shield. Under it, your body is busy making new skin.
The scab may feel itchy, but try not to pick it. If you pull it off too early, the scrape can open again.
After a week or two, the scab falls off by itself. Pink, new skin is waiting underneath.
QuestionText: What happens straight after the blood gets thick and sticky?
AnswerA: the scab falls off
AnswerD: the clot dries into a scab
